Confirmed by R. Okonkwo

Seeing the claim: how AI answers are built

Ages 8–10 · 40 minutes · 3 activities · Course version 1

  1. 1

    Warm-up: three answers, one question

    8 min

    LearnersRead three short answers to the same question and mark the one that shows where it got its facts.

    TeacherRead the answers aloud and ask the room which one they would trust, and why.

    Evidencenone collected in this activity

    ObjectivesObj 1Students can explain what an algorithm is, in their own words, with an example from everyday life.Students can explain what an algorithm is, in their own words, with an example from everyday life.

    Not evidenceA learner asking the assistant for the answer.

  2. 2

    Spotting the claim

    15 min

    LearnersUnderline the claim in a short AI-written paragraph, then write what evidence would support it.

    TeacherCirculate and ask two learners to justify an underline out loud before they write.

    Evidenceteacher observation

    ObjectivesObj 2Learners can find the claim in an AI answer and name what evidence would back it up.Learners can find the claim in an AI answer and name what evidence would back it up.

  3. 3

    Build a better answer

    17 min

    LearnersRewrite one answer so it shows its sources, then write one honest question about how the tool works.

    TeacherModel one rewrite on the board, then collect the questions for next lesson's opener.

    Evidencelearner work product

    ObjectivesObj 1Students can explain what an algorithm is, in their own words, with an example from everyday life. · Obj 3Students can ask one honest question about how an AI tool works.Students can explain what an algorithm is, in their own words, with an example from everyday life.Students can ask one honest question about how an AI tool works.

Objectives referenced

  1. 1Students can explain what an algorithm is, in their own words, with an example from everyday life. · aligns to mt_K6qtan847r (close match)
  2. 2Learners can find the claim in an AI answer and name what evidence would back it up. · aligns to mt_Qp2Ln0aVn7 (related to)
  3. 3Students can ask one honest question about how an AI tool works.

Asking the assistant a question is not evidence.
